name: Huberman sleep stack
lead: The Huberman sleep stack is a bedtime supplement combination, commonly described as magnesium threonate, apigenin and theanine, associated with Stanford neuroscientist and podcaster Andrew Huberman. People take it to fall asleep more easily and sleep more deeply, and appearance communities often treat good sleep as a foundation for skin quality, energy, training recovery and overall looks.

Andrew Huberman, an associate professor of neurobiology and ophthalmology at Stanford, launched the Huberman Lab podcast in 2021 and has published the book Protocols.[1] Wikipedia reports that he has promoted dietary supplements, which commentators such as Jonathan Jarry have criticized as poorly regulated.[1] Wikipedia's article on him does not discuss the stack itself.

Each component is sold separately: magnesium L-threonate is a magnesium salt reported to reach the brain more readily than ordinary magnesium,[2] apigenin is a plant flavone that is most abundant in chamomile flowers, parsley and celery,[3] and L-theanine is an amino acid from tea.[4] No published trial of the three-ingredient combination as a unit was found.

paras: The stack is taken in the evening. Its components are individually sold as supplements. Apigenin is a plant flavone and in chamomile flowers makes up about two thirds of the flavonoids; in laboratory work it binds the benzodiazepine site of GABA-A receptors, though researchers disagree about how it interacts with that site, and human trial data for sleep are not described in encyclopedic sources.[3] Theanine was discovered in green tea in 1949 and makes up roughly 1 to 2 percent of green tea leaf dry weight.[4] See the separate entries on magnesium threonate and on chamomile and passionflower tea for more on those ingredients.

Andrew Huberman was born in 1975 in Palo Alto, earned a Ph.D. at UC Davis in 2004, did postdoctoral work at Stanford, was an assistant professor at UC San Diego from 2011 to 2015, and became a Stanford associate professor in 2016; his research covers visual system repair and stress and anxiety interventions.[1] He launched the Huberman Lab podcast in 2021 and co-founded Scicomm Media with Robert Mohr; by 2023 the podcast was reportedly the third most popular on Spotify in the US and the most followed show on Apple Podcasts, and his YouTube channel had 7.5 million subscribers.[1] Wikipedia does not describe the stack itself, so its description here rests on how the three components are commonly bundled and on the separate articles for each.[1]

sections.h: What research says about the components
paras: The European Food Safety Authority found in 2011 insufficient evidence that theanine helps maintain normal sleep, a 2020 review suggested theanine might reduce stress and anxiety in people experiencing acute stress, and a 2025 review judged the research inconsistent and weak.[4] The US FDA treats theanine as generally recognized as safe in foods and drinks at up to 250 mg per serving.[4]
For magnesium L-threonate, Wikipedia cites one small placebo-controlled trial in healthy Chinese adults on cognition, published in Nutrients in 2022, and says nothing about sleep.[2]

Critics cited by Wikipedia say Huberman's podcast sometimes presents certainty where evidence is ambiguous and applies animal research to humans without adequate justification; New York Magazine said he often posits certainty where there is ambiguity.[1] Supporters regard his protocols as accessible summaries of neuroscience. The podcast has been sponsored by companies whose products critics consider questionable, and neuroscientist David Berson has noted that peers did not always approve of the monetization.[1]

Named commentators in Wikipedia's account include Jonathan Jarry of McGill University's Office for Science and Society, who criticised his promotion of poorly regulated supplements and the podcast's sponsor AG1; cancer biologist Joseph Zundell, who questioned extrapolation from animal research to humans; and neuroscientist David Berson, who defended the research while noting concerns about sponsorships.[1] Huberman's supporters regard the episodes as accessible summaries of neuroscience, and the podcast reportedly won a 2025 iHeartPodcast Award for Best Wellness and Fitness Podcast.[1]
No studies found of the combination.

lore.intro: The stack circulates in wellness and self-improvement communities as a nighttime routine; sleep is treated by appearance forums as a base for skin, recovery and energy.

claims.claim: The three-ingredient stack improves sleep quality and therefore how you look
claims.believers: Followers of the podcast take the stack for deeper sleep and link better sleep to skin quality, training recovery and energy.
claims.experts: No published trial has tested the three-ingredient combination; EFSA found in 2011 insufficient evidence that theanine helps maintain normal sleep, and a 2025 review judged the theanine research inconsistent and weak.[4]

claims.claim: Apigenin acts on GABA receptors to promote sleepiness
claims.believers: Supporters cite laboratory work showing apigenin binding the benzodiazepine site of GABA-A receptors.[3]
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes researchers disagree about how apigenin interacts with that site and does not describe human sleep trial data.[3]

card.summary: A bedtime trio of magnesium threonate, apigenin and theanine popularized by a podcaster; the combination itself is untested.
card.note: No trial of the combination found; supplements are loosely regulated.

quick.overview:
The Huberman sleep stack is a bedtime combination of magnesium threonate, apigenin and theanine linked to neuroscientist Andrew Huberman. People use it hoping for better sleep.

No study of the combination as a whole was found, and each ingredient has limited human sleep data.
quick.mechanism: Each ingredient is proposed to calm the nervous system through different routes; the combined effect has not been studied.
quick.risks: Individual ingredients are generally sold as supplements, which are loosely regulated. Critics of Huberman's supplement promotion say the claims outpace evidence.

chain: Evening supplements taken to aid sleep
Better recovery, energy and skin appearance
angle.text: People take the stack to improve sleep, which they connect to training recovery and fresher-looking skin. The looks effect is mediated entirely through sleep.
